mainTopic: Reading a שטר whose top and bottom lines differ: missing letters, look-alike letters, and an unclear amount
overview: This amud opens with the last line of a משנה story: the price of קינין dropped very low that same day. The גמרא then turns to the משנה about a שטר whose top and bottom lines disagree. A ברייתא teaches that the bottom line may be fixed from the top line if one letter is missing, but not two. The גמרא first suggests that two letters could be half of a four-letter name. It rejects that reason, because one letter could also be half of a two-letter name. The real reason is that two letters could be most of a three-letter name. רב פפא then rules that if the top says ספל and the bottom says קפל, the bottom decides. He asks about the reverse case, where a fly might have rubbed off the leg of a ק, and the question ends with תיקו. Finally, רב שרביא asks אביי about a שטר that says "six hundred and a זוז." אביי begins by ruling out פרוטות, and his answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The price of bird-offerings drops that same day
steps.stepSummary: The last line of the משנה's story: the price of קינין fell to a tiny amount on that very day.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the bird-nests stood that day at quarters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the final line of a משנה story. Because of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's ruling, the price of קינין (pairs of birds for offerings) dropped sharply that same day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story shows that the word 'דינרי' in the משנה means a higher-value coin than 'דינרין', since the price started high and fell to quarters. This line closes that topic so the גמרא can move to the next משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: Nests: pairs of birds brought as offerings

phrases.english: And the nests stood that day at quarters.
phrases.notes: Literally 'quarters', a very small coin amount, far below the earlier high price.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the משנה story that began earlier on the daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The price of קינין fell to a tiny amount that same day.

steps.title: A ברייתא: fix the bottom line from the top line for one letter only
steps.stepSummary: Quoting the משנה about a שטר with an upper and lower line, the גמרא brings a ברייתא: a missing letter below may be learned from the top, but not two letters.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said 'written above, etc.' The Rabbis taught: the bottom may be learned from the top for one letter, but not for two letters. For example, 'חנן' from 'חנני' and 'ענן' from 'ענני'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new משנה about a שטר that writes the same details twice, once above and once below. It quotes a ברייתא that limits how much the top line can be used to fix the bottom line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the bottom line is the main one, and the top line is there in case a letter gets erased below. The ברייתא adds a limit: the top can fill in only one missing letter. The examples show a name missing one letter at the end below (חנן) being completed from the top (חנני).

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught: introduces a ברייתא
The lower line of the שטר
The upper line of the שטר

steps.confusionAlert: The top line does not win when the two lines disagree. The bottom line is the main one; the top line is only a backup to fill in a single missing letter.

phrases.english: It is written above, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the opening words of the משנה about a שטר whose top and bottom lines differ.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: יִלְמַד הַתַּחְתּוֹן מִן הָעֶלְיוֹן – בְּאוֹת אַחַת;
phrases.english: The lower may be learned from the upper for one letter;
but not for two letters.
For example, 'Chanan' from 'Chanani',
phrases.notes: The bottom says חנן, missing one letter, and the top says חנני, so we complete it as חנני.

phrases.english: and 'Anan' from 'Anani'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the משנה about a שטר's upper and lower lines
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A missing letter in the lower line may be filled in from the upper line only if one letter is missing, not two.

steps.title: Why are two missing letters different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the ברייתא's limit of one letter.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about two letters, that we may not learn them from the top?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא allows fixing one letter but not two. This question sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the top line can be trusted for one letter, it seems it should also be trusted for two. The גמרא wants the logic that makes two letters too many.

phrases.english: What is different about two letters, that it is not allowed?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the ברייתא's rule
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason two missing letters cannot be filled in from the top line, while one can.

steps.title: Two letters might be half of a four-letter name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that two missing letters could be half of a four-letter name, which is too much to rebuild.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps it will happen to be a four-letter name, and then two letters would be half of the name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a reason: if a name has only four letters, losing two letters means losing half the name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rebuilding half of a name from the top line is too big a correction. So the חכמים made one fixed rule: whenever two letters are missing, we do not fill them in, even in longer names.

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא מִיתְרְמֵי שֵׁם בֶּן אַרְבַּע אוֹתִיּוֹת,
phrases.english: Perhaps it will happen to be a four-letter name,
and it would be half of the name.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּלְמָא מִיתְרְמֵי שֵׁם בֶּן אַרְבַּע אוֹתִיּוֹת
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Two missing letters could be half of a four-letter name, so a fixed rule bans filling in two letters.

steps.title: One letter could also be half of a two-letter name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer: by the same reasoning, one missing letter could be half of a two-letter name.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, one letter too: perhaps it will happen to be a two-letter name, and then one letter would be half of the name!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of step 4. If 'half a name' is the worry, then one missing letter should also be banned, since some names have only two letters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason given for banning two letters works just as well against one letter. That would contradict the ברייתא, which clearly allows fixing one letter. So the 'half a name' reason, as stated, cannot be enough.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא allows fixing one missing letter but not two. The 'half a name' reason for banning two letters is now under attack, because a one-letter loss could also be half of a two-letter name.

phrases.english: If so, one letter too:

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא מִיתְרְמֵי שֵׁם בֶּן שְׁתֵּי אוֹתִיּוֹת,
phrases.english: perhaps it will happen to be a two-letter name,
and it would be half of the name!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 4
steps.kashyaTarget: The 'half a name' reason given in step 4
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same logic would ban fixing even one letter, because of two-letter names. That goes against the ברייתא, which allows one letter.

steps.title: The real reason: two letters could be most of a three-letter name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the four-letter-name reason. The real worry is a three-letter name, where two missing letters would be most of the name.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the reason we cannot fill in two letters is this: maybe the name happens to have only three letters, and then two letters would be most of the name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 5 by giving a new, better reason for the ברייתא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The old reason ("half of a four-letter name") fell apart, because one letter could also be half of a two-letter name. The new idea is about the majority (רוב) of a name. We may fix a small part of a name from the top line, but not most of it. A three-letter name is common enough that חכמים made the rule for every case of two missing letters.
steps.whatToRemember: One missing letter may be filled in from the top line. Two may not, because two letters could be most of a short name.

phrases.english: Rather, with two letters, this is the reason:

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא מִיתְרְמֵי שֵׁם בֶּן שָׁלֹשׁ אוֹתִיּוֹת,
phrases.english: perhaps it will happen to be a three-letter name,
and then it would be most of the name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the reason that Step 5 knocked down.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two letters are forbidden because they could be half of a four-letter name.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two letters are forbidden because they could be most (רוב) of a three-letter name.

steps.title: ספל on top and קפל below: follow the bottom
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says it is obvious: if the top says ספל and the bottom says קפל, the bottom line decides.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: It is obvious to me that if the top says ספל (a cup) and the bottom says קפל (a garment), everything follows the bottom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new case where the top and bottom lines differ by one letter. רב פפא gives a ruling he considers obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is missing from the bottom word. It is a full, different word with a different letter. So this is not a case of "filling in" a missing letter. We simply use the משנה's normal rule that the bottom line decides.

keyTerms.meaning: A kind of garment (spelled with ק)

steps.confusionAlert: ק and ס look alike. A ק is basically a ס with an extra leg going down, so one stroke of ink makes the difference.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: It is obvious to me
that if "sefel" is written above and "kefel" below,
everything follows the bottom one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from missing letters to a letter that is different.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the bottom has a complete, different letter (קפל), the bottom decides.

steps.title: קפל on top and ספל below: maybe a fly erased the leg
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks about the reverse case. Maybe the bottom was really a ק, and a fly rubbed off its leg so it looks like a ס.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא asked: What if the top says קפל and the bottom says ספל? Do we worry that a fly rubbed off the leg of the ק, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא raises a question about the opposite case, which is not obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the bottom ס might really be a damaged ק, since a fly could have removed the small leg. If we worry about that, the bottom may not be trusted, and the top could be used to fix it. If we don't worry, the bottom decides as usual.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked (raised a question that needs solving)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa asked:
"kefel" above and "sefel" below, what is the law?
Are we concerned about a fly, or not?
phrases.notes: He means: maybe a fly landed on the wet ink and rubbed off the ק's leg, turning it into a ס.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Flips the obvious case from Step 7 into a case that is unclear.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether we suspect that a fly erased part of a letter in the bottom line.

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends רב פפא's question with תיקו: no answer is found.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes רב פפא's question without solving it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means the גמרא could not prove either side. The doubt about the fly stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand (the question is left unresolved)

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The fly question is left without an answer.

steps.title: "Six hundred and a זוז": six hundred of what?
steps.stepSummary: A שטר said "six hundred and a זוז" without naming the coin. רב שרביא asks אביי whether it means סלעים or פרוטות.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a שטר that said "six hundred and a זוז." רב שרביא sent the question to אביי: does it mean six hundred סלעים and a זוז, or six hundred פרוטות and a זוז?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case of an unclear amount in a שטר and sets up the question that אביי will answer next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The number six hundred is written, but the coin is not. A סלע is worth a lot, and a פרוטה is tiny, so the answer changes the debt enormously.

keyTerms.meaning: A זוז, a silver coin (also called a דינר)
איסתרא coins, another name for סלעים (each worth four זוזים)

phrases.english: There was a certain document in which was written:
"six hundred and a zuz",
Rav Sherevya sent it before Abaye:
Is it six hundred istira and a zuz,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא שֵׁית מְאָה פְּרִיטֵי וְזוּזָא?
phrases.english: or perhaps six hundred perutot and a zuz?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about an unclear amount, still about how to read a שטר.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which coin "six hundred" refers to when the שטר does not say.

steps.title: אביי: rule out פרוטות
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that it cannot mean פרוטות, because people turn many פרוטות into bigger coins before writing a שטר.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Take away the option of פרוטות. People do not write פרוטות in a שטר, because they add them up into bigger coins.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי begins his answer by ruling out the small-coin option. The answer continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי relies on how people normally write a שטר. Nobody writes "six hundred פרוטות"; they would convert that into larger coins. So the unnamed six hundred must be a bigger coin.

keyTerms.meaning: They add them up into larger coins

phrases.english: He said to him: Remove perutot,
since people do not write them in a document,
because they combine them into larger coins,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first half of רב שרביא's question from Step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The six hundred cannot be פרוטות, because people do not write many פרוטות in a שטר; they convert them into larger coins.
